### `RenderPipeline` tracks sprites per-`Scene`, not by raw entity id

`Game` can have several live scenes at once — the main scene plus any `loadOverlay()`-ed overlays — and each one owns its own bitECS `World`, whose entity ids independently start from 0. That means the main scene's entity `eid 3` and an overlay's entity `eid 3` are two different entities that happen to share a number. `RenderPipeline.ts` keys its sprite/texture-path tracking per `Scene` (`Map<Scene, SceneTracking>`) to avoid aliasing them — the same "never index by a raw entity id without first scoping by which world it belongs to" rule `ComponentRegistry` and `PhysicsBody`'s callback side-table already follow, just scoped by `Scene` instead of `World` since `RenderPipeline` is an external system reaching in, not a component module. Overlay sprites each get one flat, self-sorting `Container` appended to the stage after the main scene's layer containers, which is enough for draw-order-within-an-overlay without needing cross-container named layers.

That per-`Scene` scoping covers the _main_ scene too, not just overlays: `Game.unloadScene()`/`loadScene()` swap in a brand new `Scene` (a new bitECS `World`, entity ids starting at 0 again), so a single flat tracking object reused across that swap would alias the old scene's leftover Pixi sprites onto the new scene's same-numbered entities, and leave the old sprites themselves never destroyed. `_syncMain` tracks which `Scene` its tracking currently belongs to and, the moment a _different_ `Scene` object is passed in, fully disposes the previous one's tracking (`_releaseMain`, sharing the exact same per-sprite teardown `releaseOverlay`/`_pruneOverlays` already use for overlays) before starting fresh.

### `RenderPipeline` mounts a tilemap through a structural interface, not `@emptysock/tilemap`'s `Tilemap`

`RenderPipeline` stays in the core engine, since every game needs to render, not just ones with tile levels, so it cannot import `Tilemap` without making `@emptysock/engine` depend on the very module package that's supposed to depend on it. `RenderPipeline.ts` declares `TileLayerSource`, a plain structural interface covering only the `{ data: { tileWidth, tileHeight, rows, cols, tileset, layers } }` shape `mountTilemap()` actually reads; `@emptysock/tilemap`'s `Tilemap` satisfies it without either package importing the other, the same "engine depends on the interface, never a concrete implementation" pattern as `StorageAdapter`. A consequence: tests that need both a real `RenderPipeline` and a real `Tilemap` together (verifying tiles actually get mounted) live in `packages/tilemap/src/__tests__/RenderPipelineIntegration.test.ts`, since `@emptysock/tilemap` is the package that already depends on both.

### `RenderPipeline` renders `Sprite.sliceMode` 1/2 as `NineSliceSprite`/`TilingSprite`, a third per-eid map

`SceneTracking.sliced` (`eid -> { mode, node }`) is disjoint from `sprites`/`meshes`; `_syncOne()` routes a `Sprite` with `sliceMode` 1 or 2 **and** `width`/`height > 0` to `_syncSliced()` (else the untouched plain path, so mode 0 is byte-identical). Mode 1 = pixi core `NineSliceSprite` (`leftWidth`/`rightWidth`/`topHeight`/`bottomHeight` from `slice*`), mode 2 = `TilingSprite`; both sized `Sprite.width` x `height` in local space, then scaled by `Transform.scale*` like a plain sprite. Anchor: `TilingSprite.anchor`; `NineSliceSprite` has none in v8, so `pivot = (width*anchorX, height*anchorY)`. Texture load/cache/frame-path templating shares `_applyTexture`. A mode change destroys the old node and builds a new one; each branch tears down the other two maps' entry for that eid, and `_pruneUnseen`/`_releaseMain`/`releaseOverlay` cover `sliced`. Verified against the real import: an htiled `GMRBackgroundLayer` emits `Transform` (room-centre, scale 1) + `Sprite{width: room.width, sliceMode: 2, layer: "background"}`, which the default 0.5 anchor renders tiled across the room.

### `Game.attachRenderer` takes a structural interface, not the concrete `RenderPipeline`

`Game.ts` defines `SceneRenderer` (`renderFrame(main, overlays)`) as a plain interface and never imports `RenderPipeline.ts`, which in turn imports `pixi.js` and returns `HTMLCanvasElement`. `Game.ts` has to keep running under the headless testing harness in plain Node with zero DOM/Pixi involvement (the engine-environment-boundary rule), so it can only depend on the shape a renderer has, never a concrete Pixi-backed one. `Game.update()`'s render step is gated on both "a renderer is attached" and "this scene wasn't loaded with `headless: true`" — belt-and-suspenders, since a `HeadlessGame` never calls `attachRenderer` at all, but the second check means it stays safe even if something did.

### ParticleEmitter renders through a real pixi ParticleContainer, rebuilt from scratch every frame

`ParticleEmitter` (`systems/ParticleSystem.ts`) is a pure, renderer-agnostic simulation with zero pixi dependency. `RenderPipeline.mountParticles(emitter, layerName?)`/`unmountParticles(emitter)` wire it into actual gameplay rendering: one pixi core `ParticleContainer` per mounted emitter (`ParticleContainer`/`Particle` are core pixi.js exports — no new dependency), and `RenderPipeline.renderFrame()` calls a private `_syncParticles()` every frame that does `container.removeParticles()` then rebuilds the whole list from `emitter.getParticles()` — it does not diff or reuse `Particle` objects across frames. This is a deliberate tradeoff (simplicity over per-frame allocation cost); revisit it if particle counts in a real game ever become a measured bottleneck. An emitter with no `options.texture` set (the default is `""`) renders with `Texture.WHITE` rather than nothing, so a particle effect mounted before its real texture is ready is still visible. `ParticleEmitterOptions.sizeWiggle`/`.speedWiggle`/`.dirWiggle` are real per-step random fluctuations (a fresh offset drawn every step, not a fixed per-particle phase) `ParticleEmitter.update()` applies on top of the deterministic scale/velocity curve — the compat layer's `part_type_size`/`part_type_speed`/`part_type_direction` `*_wiggle` parameters translate straight onto them. `ParticleEmitterOptions.blendMode` (`"normal"`/`"add"`) is a real per-container pixi `blendMode`, set once at `mountParticles()` time — GameMaker's `part_type_blend` translates straight onto it, since pixi batches every particle in one `ParticleContainer` under a single blend mode, matching GameMaker's own per-type (not per-particle) blend setting.

### `Tilemap`'s root entity is spawned lazily by `loadInto()`, not eagerly by `register()`

`@emptysock/tilemap`'s `TilemapSystem.register(data)` is called before any `Scene` necessarily exists (a project's tilemaps are typically registered once at startup, then loaded into whichever scene needs them later) — but an `Entity` cannot exist without a real bitECS `World` to belong to. `Tilemap.entity` is therefore `null` until `TilemapSystem.loadInto(scene, name)` actually calls `scene.spawn()` and binds the result via the package-internal `_bindEntity()` — `register()` only ever constructs the map's plain data (`width`/`height`/`getLayer()`/`asGrid()`/`tileAt()` all work off `data` alone, no entity needed). Nothing outside `TilemapSystem.ts` itself reads `.entity` directly — `RenderPipeline.mountTilemap()` only needs the structural `TileLayerSource` shape (`{ data: {...} }`), never the entity. Any future system that wants to "prepare data before a scene exists, spawn a real entity once one does" should follow the same shape: a nullable entity field, set once by whichever method actually receives a live `Scene`.

### LightingSystem: real point-light falloff, and real shadow-casting occlusion

`LightingSystem` (`systems/LightingSystem.ts`) collects every enabled `LightSource` (a point light with `radius`/`colour`/`intensity`/`falloff`, position read from `Transform` plus an offset, same convention `Sprite`/`PhysicsBody` use) into a plain, framework-agnostic `LightSample[]`; `RenderSystem.syncLighting()` turns that list into pixel output — a real offscreen lightmap `RenderTexture` built from concentric additively-blended `Graphics` circles per light, composited over the scene via `pixi-filters`' real `SimpleLightmapFilter` (see that method's own doc comment for why this, not a hand-rolled multi-light shader, is the library-level primitive this system is built on).

**Shadow-casting is real, not aspirational.** A `LightSource` on one side of a wall no longer illuminates straight through it — the "dark cave with torches" case this system exists for. `components/LightOccluder.ts` marks an entity as a light-blocker: a plain axis-aligned box (`width`/`height`, positioned via `Transform` + offset, `enabled` toggle — the same shape `LightSource` itself already uses, deliberately, so the two components read as obvious siblings). This is a dedicated component, not a reuse of `Meta.solid` — `Meta.solid` is GameMaker's collision-query flag with no geometry of its own (`place_meeting`/`place_free` instead derive an AABB from `spriteHalfExtents()`), so a real box a light can actually cast a shadow from has nowhere to live on `Meta` regardless; once a dedicated component is needed for the geometry anyway, keeping "blocks light" as its own concern (rather than folding it into `Meta.solid`) also keeps two genuinely-different-in-general properties honestly independent — an iron gate can be solid for collision and translucent to light, a magic ward can block light with nothing solid to collide with. An ordinary wall that should do both simply carries both components on the same entity, the ordinary ECS answer.

**The algorithm** (`systems/LightOcclusion.ts`, pure geometry, no pixi import — stays inside the engine environment boundary, fully unit-testable under plain Node/Vitest) is the standard "visibility polygon from occluder-segment endpoints" technique: for each light, cast a ray from its centre at the angle of every nearby occluder-segment endpoint (plus a hair before/after each one, so a ray grazing a corner samples both sides of it), find the closest segment intersection along each ray via the standard cross-product ray/segment parametrisation, clipped to the light's own radius (which doubles as its natural far clip), and connect the resulting hit points in angle order into a polygon. Between occluders, extra angle samples evenly spaced around the full circle (`LightingSystemOptions.raySamples`, default 32) keep an unoccluded arc looking like an arc rather than a straight polygon chord. `LightOcclusion.test.ts` and `LightingSystem.test.ts` assert this against real, hand-worked-out geometry (a point directly behind a wall segment is not in the resulting polygon; a point beside it is; a light close enough to a short wall illuminates past its ends) via a real point-in-polygon check, not "renders without throwing".

**Spatial culling, and the honest remaining perf caveat.** `LightingSystem.collectLights()` gathers every enabled `LightOccluder` once per call (not once per light), then per light runs `boxWithinReach()` — an O(1) AABB-vs-circle distance test — before any ray work, so a wall on the far side of the level never enters a torch's ray-casting pass. Worst case is still `O(lights × occluders × rays)`, the same shape `RenderSystem.renderMultiCamera()`'s own doc comment already names for its N-render-pass cost; for the "5-10 torches, dozens of wall segments" dungeon scale this system targets, that's a few thousand cheap ray/segment tests per frame — a scene leaning on hundreds of simultaneously-occluded lights still needs real device profiling before shipping, the same honest caveat this codebase's other N-pass rendering features already carry rather than pretending is free.

**Rendering side**: `LightSample.visibility` is `null` when no occluder was within a light's radius — the common case — which is what keeps an occluder-free scene byte-for-byte identical to the pre-occlusion implementation: `RenderSystem`'s `buildLightGraphics()` renders the ordinary un-masked circular falloff whenever it sees `null`. When `visibility` is a real polygon, `buildLightGraphics()` builds a second `Graphics` filling that polygon and sets it as the light `Graphics`' `.mask` — a genuine pixi geometric mask (not a CSS/filter approximation), in the same local coordinate space, deliberately never added to `_lightMapContainer`'s own display tree (pixi masks against another display object's geometry without requiring it to be in the scene graph, as long as both share the same coordinate space, which they do here).

### GMS2 surface/blend cutout lighting (`compat/gmlSurfaces.ts`): a pixi-free backend interface, `RenderPipeline` builds the render textures

Grepped every available real sample project source for `light`/`surface_set_target`/`bm_subtract`/`gpu_set_blendmode`/`bm_add`: only the separate "camera" project (`obj_lighting`/`obj_light`/`obj_torches`/`obj_mask`/`obj_sunburst`) uses it, and none of the other real projects does. The technique is the classic darkness surface (light-grey fill, lights drawn with `bm_subtract` as cutouts, then the surface drawn over the view with `bm_subtract`); `bm_add` for glows. It maps onto the existing engine-native path (`LightingSystem` ambient level + `LightSource` point/cone lights + `LightOccluder` shadows) for new engine code, but a GML-authored surface path was genuinely missing, so it is now real: `gpu_set_blendmode`/`draw_set_blend_mode` (`bm_normal/add/max/subtract` = 0-3; `gpu_set_blendmode_ext` is a warned no-op — arbitrary factors are not modelled), `surface_create/exists/free/set_target/reset_target`, `draw_surface`, `draw_clear(_alpha)`, `draw_ellipse(_color)`/`draw_triangle(_color)` (flat first-colour fill, no gradient), and legacy `view_xview/yview/wview/hview` (read from view 0's camera, index ignored).

Layering: `compat/gmlSurfaces.ts` imports no pixi; it defines `GmlSurfaceBackend` and swaps `ctx.drawTarget` in and out (a per-`ctx` stack, so targets nest). `GmlActionContext.surfaces` is the injection point; `RenderPipeline.surfaces` (a private `PixiSurfaceBackend`, one `RenderTexture` per surface) is wired by `GmsProjectRuntime.buildContext()`. `beginTarget` returns a `PixiGmlDrawTarget` over a scratch `Graphics`; `endTarget` renders it into the texture (`renderer.render({container, target, clear})`, accumulating over prior contents unless `draw_clear` set `pendingClear`). A `PixiGmlDrawTarget` blend change starts a new child `Graphics` segment carrying the pixi blend mode, because a `Graphics` has one blend mode; sprites/text added afterwards inherit it. `draw_surface` adds a `Sprite` of the surface texture to the current segment, so `bm_subtract` on the final draw is real. Without a backend every call is a safe no-op and `surface_create` returns `-1`. Transpiler: threaded via `THREADED_CTX_ONLY`, `bm_*` via `GML_MISC_CONSTANTS`, the shape draws via `_ctx.drawTarget && GmlActions.draw_*(_ctx.drawTarget, ...)`. GPU compositing is not verified headless. Tests: `gmlSurfaces.test.ts` (routing, render-target call incl. clear colour, segment blend modes, plus a `LightingSystem` ambient/cone/occluder darkness+cutout coverage test), `gms2-transpile.test.ts` ("GMS2 cutout lighting").

### PostProcessSystem's layer filters become real pixi Filters, not just CSS strings

`PostProcessSystem.setLayerFilter(layerId, opts)` stores a framework-agnostic `LayerFilterOptions` (a type string plus params) and can render a CSS-string approximation via `cssFilterForLayer()` for a host that draws a layer as a DOM element. `RenderSystem.syncPostProcessLayerFilters(postProcess)` translates those same options into a real PixiJS filter for the actual WebGL/WebGPU-rendered layers: it reads `postProcess.layerFilters` and builds/updates one real `Filter` per layer id via `addLayerShaderFilter()` (an engine-owned side-table, keyed by layer id, the same pattern `PhysicsBody`'s callback side-table uses). The effect-to-library mapping is `blur` → pixi.js core's `BlurFilter`; `brightness`/`contrast`/`saturate`/`hue-rotate`/`invert`/`colour-grade` → pixi.js core's `ColorMatrixFilter` via its chainable convenience methods; `colourblind` → `ColorMatrixFilter` with `PostProcessSystem`'s own `COLOURBLIND_MATRICES` CVD-simulation coefficients embedded directly into the 5x4 matrix (the same coefficients `cssFilterForLayer()`'s SVG `feColorMatrix` fallback already uses, so the two code paths can never visually disagree); `outline` → `pixi-filters@6.1.5`'s `OutlineFilter`. One filter instance is cached per layer id and only rebuilt when that layer's filter _type_ changes — an unchanged type just gets its params re-applied in place — so calling this every frame doesn't reallocate a GPU filter per frame. `CustomShaderFilter`/`LightingSystem` need no equivalent wiring — both already construct a plain pixi `Filter` directly and go through the same pre-existing `addLayerShaderFilter()`.

`addLayerShaderFilter`/`removeLayerShaderFilter` null-coalesce `container.filters` to `[]` before spreading/filtering — PixiJS's own type says `readonly Filter[]` (never `null`/`undefined`), but a freshly constructed `Container` actually has it unset at runtime, so the very first filter ever attached to any layer via either method would otherwise throw. If you hit a PixiJS type claiming something is never null/undefined, verify the runtime behaviour of a fresh instance before trusting the type.

### GMS2 shaders: real per-entity pixi Filters via a module-level `ShaderRegistry`, not a tint approximation

`systems/ShaderRegistry.ts` (no pixi import) is a module-level `Map` keyed by GameMaker shader name (`registerGmlShader(id, {vertexSrc, fragmentSrc})`, module-level like `registerGmlBehavior` because `shader_set(sh_white)` addresses shaders by global name with no `Game` in reach). Registration normalises CR/CRLF to LF. The generated `assets/<name>.shader.ts` now imports `@emptysock/engine` and calls `registerGmlShader(name, XShader)` at module load, so importing the asset is what registers it; `gms2-shader-import.ts`'s translator also normalises CRLF/lone-CR itself (found in the real `sh_white.fsh`: a lone `\r` after a `//` comment could swallow the next declaration).

**The importer's vertex stage cannot be used as a Filter vertex.** Reading pixi 8.21's `defaultFilter.vert` against `CustomShaderFilter`'s contract found they differ: a pixi Filter's quad is positioned via `uOutputFrame`/`uOutputTexture`/`uInputSize`, and `uProjectionMatrix`/`uWorldTransformMatrix`/`uTransformMatrix` (what the translated vertex and `DEFAULT_CUSTOM_SHADER_VERTEX` use) are never set for a filter, which would collapse the quad. The importer only accepts the standard passthrough position transform, so `toFilterVertexSource()` replaces the position half with pixi's own `filterVertexPosition` maths and carries over only the `out` varyings (texcoord-named -> `filterTextureCoord`, everything else `vec4(1.0)`). `CustomShaderOptions.adaptVertex: true` now applies that substitution inside `CustomShaderFilter` itself (opt-in, because a hand-authored vertex stage already written against the filter contract, and the ShaderEditor default, must stay untouched), so the per-layer path is fixed too: `buildGmlShaderFilter(id)` (`CustomShaderFilter.ts`) is the one builder for a registered shader (adapted vertex, uniforms declared) shared by the per-entity `RenderPipeline.resolveShaderFilter` and the new per-layer `RenderSystem.addLayerGmlShader(layer, id)` (returns the filter for `removeLayerShaderFilter`; `syncLayerGmlShaders()`, called from `render()`, copies later `shader_set_uniform_*` writes in when the registry version changes). Passing an importer shader's `vertexSrc` to a raw `createCustomShaderFilter` without `adaptVertex` still collapses the quad. Tests: `CustomShaderFilter.test.ts` (adaptVertex, `buildGmlShaderFilter`), `RenderPipelineShaders.test.ts` (per-layer block). `CustomShaderFilter` gained `options.uniforms` (declared up front — pixi needs uniform types at construction; `parseShaderUniforms()` derives them from `uniform float/int/vecN` declarations in the fragment source) and `setUniform()`.

**Attachment.** `Sprite.shader` (plain string, `""` = none) is the data; `RenderPipeline._syncOne()` sets the tracked pixi sprite's `.filters` to `[filter]` via `_applySpriteShader()` (no write when already correct, so steady state allocates nothing) and clears it to `null` when unset. `resolveShaderFilter(id)` builds one `CustomShaderFilter` per shader id lazily, shared by every entity and every draw call (filters are shareable), rebuilt only if the id is re-registered, destroyed with the pipeline. Plain-sprite path only: nine-slice/tiled/`Projection3D` nodes and vector shapes/text drawn on a Draw `Graphics` are not filtered.

**Two paths for `shader_set`, chosen by whether a Draw event is running** (`compat/gmlShaders.ts`, split out of `gmlActions.ts`). Inside `onDraw`/`onDrawGui` (`ctx.drawTarget` set — the real `obj_pShootable` shape: `shader_set(sh_white); draw_self(); shader_reset();`) it calls `GmlDrawTarget.setShader()`, and `PixiGmlDrawTarget` puts the filter on each sprite-shaped draw child until reset — it cannot go through `Sprite.shader`, because set and reset both happen inside one Draw call, before any render sync. Outside a Draw event it writes/clears `Sprite.shader`. Either way a per-`(World, eid)` side-table remembers the entity's active shader (cleared by `clearGmlActionState`). An unregistered shader name is a one-time warning and an unfiltered draw, never a throw. The real project output was re-imported and read: `obj_enemy`/`obj_enemyBig.behavior.ts` (inherited `obj_pShootable` Draw) emit `GmlActions.shader_set(_entity, _ctx, "sh_white")`, and `sh_white.shader.ts` is LF-only with the registration call.

**Uniforms are per shader id, shared by every entity using it** — GameMaker's own are global-until-changed state on the bound shader, so this matches rather than approximates; per-entity values would need one Filter per entity. `shader_get_uniform(shader, name)` returns the name as the handle; `shader_set_uniform_f/_i/_f_array/_i_array(handle, ...)` write into the calling entity's _active_ shader (GML's "currently bound shader" semantics; a warned no-op with none set). Writes bump a registry version and `resolveShaderFilter` copies them into the filter's resources only when the version changed. `shader_is_compiled` reports registration only. `gms2-transpile.ts` quotes the bare `shader_set` argument, threads the four setters, and gained `setGmlShaderNames`/a `"shader"` kind in the project-wide asset-name registry (cross-kind collisions stay unresolved, as for every kind).

**GPU compilation is not verified.** Headless Node has no WebGL context, so tests cover wiring (which Filter lands on which sprite/draw child, registry, uniform copy, transpile output, import output), never pixels or GLSL compile success; the filter-vertex contract above is from reading pixi's source, not from running it on a GPU. Tests: `ShaderRegistry.test.ts`, `gmlShaders.test.ts`, `RenderPipelineShaders.test.ts`, `gms2-transpile.test.ts` ("shader_set / shader_reset / uniforms"), `gms2-shader-import.test.ts`.

### Real-GPU verification: `packages/engine/scripts/gpu-verify.mjs`

Headless vitest mocks the renderer, so GLSL and blend behaviour were never exercised. `gpu-verify.mjs` bundles a harness with rolldown, runs it in headless Chromium (swiftshader WebGL2) and pixel-asserts `RainGlassFilter`, the importer's `sh_white` via `Sprite.shader`, `BitmapText` from the real `fnt_menu` atlas and the surface/`bm_subtract` cutout (details and screenshots: `docs/gpu-verify/`). It found three real bugs, now fixed and worth remembering: (1) a pixi `Filter`'s vertex stage has only `aPosition` (no `aUV`/projection matrices), so `DEFAULT_CUSTOM_SHADER_VERTEX` and the rain vertex use pixi's filter position maths and `CustomShaderFilter` auto-adapts a sprite-style vertex source (`adaptVertex` is now inferred, `false` opts out); (2) filter uniforms must be a `UniformGroup` handed to the `Filter` constructor, never a plain object assigned to `resources` afterwards (pixi never uploads it, every uniform read 0), and tests read `.uniforms[name]`; (3) `"subtract"` is a pixi advanced blend mode: `RenderPipeline` imports `pixi.js/advanced-blend-modes` and `RenderSystem` passes `useBackBuffer: true`, otherwise `bm_subtract` silently renders as normal. A filter applied to the render root itself is ignored by pixi; wrap it in a child container. Timing on swiftshader is CPU rasterisation, not GPU cost; real device profiling is still open.

---

### Rain: `RainGlassFilter` (single-pass lens droplets with fading trails) and `rainParticlePreset`

`RainGlassFilter`'s fragment shader (exported as `RAIN_GLASS_FRAGMENT` so tests can assert on it) is one pass with no loops: two hashed droplet grids, refraction via a procedural fake normal, and a fading vertical trail behind the falling grid's drops (drops drift down-screen; the trail sits above). `rainParticlePreset({ width, density, wind })` returns `ParticleEmitterOptions` for world-space rain (line emitter above the view). Not physically-based; no drop merging.
